extracted.intended_audience: writers of periodical/moral essays and general readers interested in tasteful, instructive humour
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short moral/entertaining periodical papers that instruct without corrupting, balancing wit and seriousness to reach different reader temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish constitutional good-nature from moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not praise mere good-nature that arises from bodily constitution as if it were moral merit; distinguish natural temperament ('milkiness of blood') from deliberate moral virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist should test whether apparent goodness is stable and morally grounded rather than a transient physical temperament. Treat constitutional ease as admirable insofar as it is the groundwork for moral good-nature, but not as a substitute for virtue or praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature must show steadiness and uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: A true moral good-nature acts with steadiness and uniformity in sickness and health, in prosperity and adversity; transient, situational amiability is not true philanthropy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware examples of temporary good-humour (e.g. the solicitor who petitions when a great man is at dinner). Use steadiness across states of life as a test when depicting or praising a character's benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature must operate according to reason and duty (discriminate objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral good-nature should make distinctions among its objects — it must not relieve indiscriminately the deserving and undeserving or give to the idle equally with the indigent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying charity or benevolence, show that the benefactor exercises judgment and choice, directing help to proper objects rather than acting promiscuously or by accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature requires willingness to sacrifice for others
rubrics_metrics.description: A test of moral good-nature is whether one will exert it to personal disadvantage — risking fortune, reputation, health, or ease for the benefit of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatize or evaluate characters by their readiness to endure real cost on behalf of others; mere pleasantness without sacrifice is not full virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudent management of charity (proportionate, non-prejudicial giving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with more than necessary should set aside a certain proportion of income for the poor, but should do so with prudence so as not to harm friends or relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete practices (e.g. Eugenius's rule to live on less and set aside a tenth, fasting-abstinence to augment charity, redirecting leisure money) as exemplary techniques. Emphasize making charitable giving sustainable and mindful of family obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instructive exempla and sacred texts to moralize
rubrics_metrics.description: Support moral arguments with striking examples and scriptural passages (e.g. Job, Matthew, Proverbs) to persuade and illustrate the virtues discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral essays, employ well-chosen extracts and examples to set models for readers; such authorities strengthen the claim and provide vivid pictures of virtue in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance tones to serve two reader types (mercurial and saturnine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to vary content between wit/humour (for the mercurial readers) and sober morality/sense (for the saturnine readers), because always writing in one tone will lose half the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate or blend diverting and instructive material so readers of differing temperaments are engaged. Let light pieces sometimes carry serious lessons and serious pieces occasionally yield to mirth to attract broader readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make humour serve instruction and remain innocent
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughing in writing is acceptable only insofar as it instructs; if mirth ceases to be instructive it must at least remain innocent and not corrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppress or avoid strokes of raillery that have a remote tendency to corrupt manners; avoid ill-nature and personal injury in jests. The writer should deliberately omit tempting but improper lines (''discreetly blot'').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise editorial restraint (censor / 'castrate' improper material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or tone down parts of submissions or letters that are likely to be injurious, corrupting, or otherwise improper for public print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing correspondences or entertaining anecdotes, actively excise passages that tend toward ill-nature or corruption. The author may 'castrate' letters to preserve innocence and public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use entertainment as a means to lead readers to deeper reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Light entertainments can 'insnare' unthinking readers into sentiments of wisdom and virtue, preparing them for more serious study; dispersing melancholy with humour can be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pieces so that amusement often opens the way for profitable thought — e.g., diverting readers into a train of reflection or relieving gloom to make moral instruction more palatable.
